---
title: Baking bread with commercial yeast
lang: en
free: true
---
Commercial yeast—available as instant granules or active dry packets—allows bakers to produce a well-risen loaf in a fraction of the time sourdough requires. The yeast, _Saccharomyces cerevisiae_, is cultivated in controlled industrial conditions, then dried and packaged at consistent cell counts. This predictability is its main advantage: a teaspoon added to flour, water, and salt begins producing carbon dioxide within minutes, not hours.

## Activating and mixing the dough

Active dry yeast benefits from proofing in warm water (38–43 °C) for five to ten minutes until foam appears, confirming viability. Instant yeast can be mixed directly into dry ingredients. Once water is added, gluten develops through kneading—typically eight to ten minutes by hand. A smooth, elastic dough that springs back when poked is ready for its first rise.

## Quick rise and baking

At room temperature the dough doubles in roughly one to two hours. A brief second rise after shaping—called the proof—builds oven spring. Unlike long fermentation, this rapid schedule leaves little time for complex flavour compounds to form, so the crumb is mild and pillowy rather than tangy. A hot oven (220–230 °C) with steam in the first ten minutes produces a crisp golden crust.
